research.headline: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
research.summary: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging.

research.headline: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
research.summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures.

research.headline: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
research.summary: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test.

frontier.headline: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism
frontier.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave. The breakthrough offers a promising new path toward understanding exotic quantum materials and developing future electronic technologies.

frontier.headline: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
frontier.summary: IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing.

frontier.headline: Simple design of adaptive protocols for quantum metrology with limited data
frontier.summary: Recent sensing experiments have used a Bayesian notion of precision gain to adapt control parameters for fixed measurements. Here, we advocate a simple design principle based on Personick's minimum mean square loss formalism to extend this procedure in order to include measurement optimisation, determining the optimal measurement for each probe and providing a prior-dependent precision gain to optimise the probe itself. This offers a Bayesian counterpart to protocol design based on the Fisher information, with a similar algebraic structure but incorporating the full prior.

frontier.headline: Two messages suffice for quantum interactive proof systems
frontier.summary: Quantum interactive proof systems can be parallelized to three messages, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), perhaps their most striking distinction from classical counterparts. In this work, we establish that any quantum interactive proof system can further be parallelized to two messages, with the verifier sending halves of EPR pairs (``quantum public coins'') and, after the prover's response, using only stoquastic verification. Technically, we strengthen ${\sf QIP}(3) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}$ of Jain, Ji, Upadhyay, and Watrous (JACM, 2011) and fully characterize two-message quantum interactive proof systems by proving \[ {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf StoqAM} = {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM} = {\sf QIP}(2) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}.

frontier.headline: Small-world networks yield tunable quantum codes at short circuit depth
frontier.summary: Monitored random quantum circuits naturally generate quantum error-correcting codes. We generate quantum codes with tunable properties by implementing random Clifford circuits on Watts--Strogatz `small-world' networks and tailor code properties via three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth. On fully rewired networks, circuits of logarithmic depth produce codes with a finite rate and an extensive mean contiguous distance with failure probability substantially lower than codes produced from local circuits.

voices.headline: Air Is Easing Out of the AI Bubble
voices.summary: ET on November 23, 2026 This should be a bullish time for investors in the AI business. Nvidia, which designs most of the chips that have driven the AI boom, just reported that its sales and profits doubled year-over-year, and that it’s on pace to grow another 75 percent next year. The industry as a whole, Nvidia said, has a backlog of $2.5 trillion in future orders, meaning that demand remains strong.

voices.headline: ‘Our History Is Better Than Anybody Else’s’
voices.summary: F or years now, Donald Trump and the MAGA movement have cast the United States as the heir to and defender of Western civilization. In the second Trump administration, this sort of grandiose rhetoric has increased; the administration presents itself as the lone bulwark against the barbarians at the gates who would annihilate everything good about the world. “Our lineage and our legacy hails back to Athens, to Rome,” Stephen Miller, Trump’s longtime adviser and new chief of staff, said at the funeral for the assassinated conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

voices.headline: Why Trump Rescued Jensen Huang
voices.summary: A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scandal. Last night, The New York Times reported that a Chinese woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s once and future chief executive, was in regular contact with China’s spy agency . The woman, Alice Huang, may have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s decision to sell advanced chips to companies that transferred them to China.

voices.headline: A New Age of Sail
voices.summary: Photographs by Peter Fisher For a few hours , it was magical. The Neoliner Origin, the world’s largest sailing cargo ship, was cruising across the Atlantic Ocean powered by nothing but wind. Four huge sails billowed from masts towering 90 meters above the waterline.
